entry.title: Post’s Functional Completeness Theorem: Is Negation Sufficient for Universality?

link.title: Post’s Functional Completeness Theorem: Is Negation Sufficient for Universality?

entry.content:
Hi! I’m Aryan, an undergraduate at UCLA studying mathematics and computer engineering. In this post, I discuss Post’s Functional Completeness Theorem (Emil Post, 1941).

This post was mostly motivated by a question on my CS 181 Theory of Computation Problem Set:

(Boaz Barak Intro TCS Exercise 3.4) Prove that for every $n$-bit input circuit $C$ that contains only AND and OR gates, as well as gates that compute the constant functions 0 and 1, $C$ is monotone, in the sense that if $x, x’ \in \lbrace 0, 1 \rbrace^n$ satisfy $x_i \leq x’_i$ for every $i \in [n]$, then $C(x) \leq C(x’)$. Conclude that the set ${\text{AND}, \text{OR}, 0, 1}$ is not universal.

I was attempting this problem and thought about the universality of {AND, NOT} as well as {NAND} (one can show that {AND, NOT} is universal by using the universality of NAND and vice versa). In generally all cases of universality of gate sets, some form of negation ($\neg$) is incorporated even if not explicitly stated in the function definition. For example, the gate set $\mathcal{F} = \lbrace \implies, 0 \rbrace$ is universal even though NOT is not explicitly used. However, one can easily deduce that the following holds: $a \implies 0 = \neg a$. The negation appears both explicitly and implicitly in many such cases of universality of gate sets and I was curious as to whether negation was necessary for universality or if my observations were purely by chance. This led me to learn about Post’s Functional Completeness Theorem which I now discuss below!
entry.summary: Negation is Necessary but not Sufficient for Universality

entry.title: The Physical-Extended Church-Turing Thesis in a Quantum Sense

link.title: The Physical-Extended Church-Turing Thesis in a Quantum Sense

entry.content:
Hi! I’m Aryan, an undergraduate at UCLA studying mathematics and computer engineering. In this post, I discuss the Physical-Extended Church-Turing Thesis (Alonzo Church, Alan Turing, Stephen Kleene, 1930s).

This post was mostly motivated by curiosity. In class, a short discussion over the philosophical realizations of the Church-Turing Thesis (CTT) and its validity (no proof!) in both the classical and quantum sense seemed intriguing to me. It’s believed that the Physical-Extended CTT is true in a classical sense and false in a quantum sense (but why? that’s what we discuss in the blog :D), however, one can easily construct (or I suppose, extend) a Quantum-Extended Church-Turing Thesis which allows CTT to be true in a quantum sense as well (we discuss this too).
entry.summary: Is the Physical-Extended Church-Turing Thesis, often believed to be true in classical computers, also true in quantum computers?
